name: Museo Revoltella
funding: Civic museum operated by the Comune di Trieste, founded on the bequest of Baron Pasquale Revoltella, who left his palace, art collection and a substantial income to the city. The pages read gave no current budget or amounts.
watch: Civic museum in three connected buildings. Finestre sull'Arte wrote on 8 July 2022 that Trieste's civic museums had been without a scientific director for at least five years, and il manifesto on 25 February 2023 called the Revoltella a museum 'oggi senza un direttore'.

overview: The Museo Revoltella is a modern art museum in Trieste occupying the Revoltella Palace, the Brunner Palace and the smaller Basevi building, which houses the administration (museum website).

It grew out of an institution founded in 1872: Baron Pasquale Revoltella (1795 to 1869), a Venetian-born entrepreneur and financier, left his palace, art collection and a substantial income to the city, and the palace became the museum under his will, managed by a Board of Trustees (museum website).

What is there: the founder's collection, now mainly shown in the Revoltella Palace, grew to include 19th century painters such as Francesco Hayez and Domenico Morelli and 20th century artists such as Giorgio Morandi, Carlo Carra and Lucio Fontana (museum website). The pages read gave no object count.

Archive: a library in the Revoltella Palace, listed as the Biblioteca Sergio Molesi, holds books and travel memoirs including accounts of Revoltella's 1861 visit to Egypt; the page did not describe an archive (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Museo Revoltella: municipal museum funded by the Comune di Trieste from the founder's bequest onwards.
funding: The Comune di Trieste is named as the museum's operator; Revoltella's bequest originally provided income for it (museum website).
No reporting found in the pages read of current grants, sponsors or accounts.

red_flags.heading: No museum director
points: Finestre sull'Arte reported on 8 July 2022 that news of the abolition of the post of director of the Trieste Civic Museums was in fact a reshuffle in a new municipal organisation chart presented by assessor Stefano Avian and director general Fabio Lorenzut, which separates museums from libraries; its author Federico Giannini wrote that since 2017 the civic museums had reported to a single manager, Laura Carlini, and that they had been without a scientific director for at least five years (Finestre sull'Arte, 8 July 2022).

Giannini linked the reorganisation to rationalisation of expenses and cited the ICOM recommendation of 2011 and Ministerial Decree 113/2018, which require a museum director; he reported no resolution (Finestre sull'Arte, 8 July 2022).

Il manifesto, in a print piece of 25 February 2023 by Marinella Salvi, calls the Revoltella a civic museum 'oggi senza un direttore'; only the summary of the article was read, and it gives no reply from the city (il manifesto, 25 February 2023).

details.bottom_line: The Revoltella is paid by the city of Trieste from the founder's bequest tradition; the pages read gave no budget. The contested point is the long absence of a museum director.

name: Pinacoteca Agnelli
funding: The pages read did not state who funds it.
watch: A museum on the roof of the Lingotto, the former Fiat factory, housing 25 works collected by Giovanni Agnelli and Marella Caracciolo and donated in 2002; Sarah Cosulich became director with the programme that opened on 27 May 2022.

overview: A museum on the roof of the Lingotto in Turin, in the five-storey Scrigno designed by Renzo Piano and built in 2002 (Artribune, 12 March 2022).
The collection was donated in 2002 by Giovanni Agnelli and Marella Caracciolo's collection (Artribune, 12 March 2022).
What is there: 25 masterpieces from the 18th to the 20th century (Artribune, 12 March 2022).

The renewed museum opened on 27 May 2022 with a Picasso and Dora Maar exhibition developed with the Fondation Beyeler and a Sylvie Fleury show, under director Sarah Cosulich (Artribune; Finestre sull'Arte, March 2022).
details.funding_verdict: Pinacoteca Agnelli: funders not stated in the pages read.
funding: The pages read do not say who owns or funds the Pinacoteca, and name no foundation or sponsor.
No reporting found of amounts in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The pages read give the collection's origin as a family donation but not who pays for operations, which needs the museum's own accounts.
details.website: https://www.pinacoteca-agnelli.it/en/ (checked 2026-11-18; the page returned only a list of headings)

name: Reggia di Caserta
funding: A state site on a cultura.gov.it domain; the pages read did not state its budget or funders.
watch: The Bourbon royal palace begun in 1752 to a design by Luigi Vanvitelli and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997. Its first director under the 2016 reform, Mauro Felicori, was at the centre of a union row in March 2016 and left on 31 October 2018 at the retirement age.
records_note: Its site has an Amministrazione trasparente section; no accounts were opened.

overview: A royal palace complex at Piazza Carlo di Borbone, Caserta, with the Palazzo Reale, Parco Reale, Giardino Inglese, Bosco di San Silvestro and Acquedotto Carolino (museum website).

Carlo di Borbone bought the Caserta fief in 1750 for 489,348.13 ducats, the architect was Luigi Vanvitelli and the king laid the first stone on 20 January 1752; the Reggia, the Acquedotto Carolino and the Belvedere di San Leucio have been UNESCO World Heritage since 1997 (museum website).

What is there: royal apartments, the Teatro di Corte, the Cappella Palatina, the Gran Galleria, the Biblioteca Palatina and 123 hectares of park; the collections page is being digitised (museum website).

Archive: the historic archive, set up by Ferdinando IV by a Real Dispaccio of 25 May 1784, holds more than 10,000 units from the 15th to the mid 20th century, about 5,000 units on the Bourbon sites from 1860 to about 1950 and 402 volumes of notarial protocols; access is free after registering with the Archivio di Stato di Caserta, reading room Monday to Friday 8:30 to 16:00 (museum website, archive page).
details.funding_verdict: Reggia di Caserta: public, a state site; amounts not stated in the pages read.
funding: The pages read did not state a budget, ticket income or sponsors; the site links an Amministrazione trasparente section (museum website).
A restoration plan of about 60 million euros followed the 2012 collapses and was due to finish in 2020 (Artribune, August 2018).

red_flags.heading: Labour dispute
points: In early March 2016 unions UILPA, UGL-Intesa, USB and the RSU wrote to the Ministry about the new director Mauro Felicori, raising unclear office hours, security staff moved to administrative tasks and rooms lent free to third parties (Finestre sull'Arte, 6 March 2016).

Il Mattino di Napoli ran the headline that the director works too much and puts the Reggia at risk, and Matteo Renzi quoted it on Facebook; Felicori called the letter a gesture of defiance; the unions said they had never accused him of overworking. Finestre sull'Arte argued the headline reversed the letter's meaning (Finestre sull'Arte, 6 March 2016).
The page reports no formal resolution.

red_flags.heading: Governance
points: Felicori announced his departure on 6 August 2018 and left on 31 October 2018 on reaching the retirement age, about a year before his mandate ended; the criticisms listed were the Cavallerizze lent to the mozzarella consortium and a private wedding with 250 guests, and a 2017 appeal against his appointment was rejected by the regional administrative court (Artribune, August 2018).

details.bottom_line: The State owns and runs it and the pages read give no accounts. The documented rows are from 2016 to 2018 under Felicori; no 2022 to 2026 dispute was found in the pages read.

name: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art
funding: Municipal, run by the Kanazawa Art Promotion Foundation.
why_flagged: Gold member Kanazawa Energy is a city-gas utility, 48% Hokuriku Electric and 43% Toho Gas. Iwatani Central Hokuriku (LPG) also listed.
records_note: Kanazawa 21 posts its 2025 annual report and names its supporting members by tier undated.
affiliations_note: Partners with Kanazawa College of Art and the Oku-Noto Triennale committee under 2019 agreements, and with the Kanazawa Noh Museum and Yuwaku Sousaku no Mori since 2006. Member of CIMAM.
highlight: SANAA's circular glass building holds Leandro Erlich's permanent illusion installation 'The Swimming Pool'.

overview: City museum of contemporary art in central Kanazawa, near the Kenroku-en garden and the Ishikawa Prefectural Museum of Art (Wikipedia).
Opened on 9 October 2004. The city of Kanazawa owns the project and the public interest foundation Kanazawa Arts Creation Foundation runs the museum (Japanese Wikipedia).
Building: designed by Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa of SANAA, A circular, mostly glass structure about 112.5 metres across, built from April 2002 to August 2004.

What is there: a collection of work made since 1980, long-term installations such as Leandro Erlich's Swimming Pool (2004), temporary exhibitions, a library, a lecture hall, a cafe-restaurant and a museum shop.

Visiting: entering the building is free. Exhibition tickets vary by show. The exhibition zone is open 10:00 to 18:00 (to 20:00 on Fridays and Saturdays) and closed on Mondays and over the New Year (museum.or.jp directory).
Closure: Japanese Wikipedia reports a city plan to close the museum from May 2027 to about March 2028 for repairs.
details.funding_verdict: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art: mainly public (the city of Kanazawa), with a corporate and individual membership scheme
funding: The city of Kanazawa owns the project and the foundation it funds manages the museum (Japanese Wikipedia).

Sustain membership: the museum's members page lists companies and individuals by tier. The list carries no date; the only year on the page is the 2024 copyright line in the footer. Platinum (500,000 yen a year per unit): My Book Service Co. Gold (300,000 yen a year per unit): Kanazawa Energy, Impress Art Business Division, Fukumitsuya and Dimple. Standard (50,000 yen a year per unit): about 100 further companies and bodies, including Hokkoku Bank, Kanazawa Chamber of Commerce, Nikkiso, Iwatani Central Hokuriku and the SANAA office. The page does not say how many units each member holds. Dues count as donations to the foundation.

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuels (gas utility among top-tier members)
points: Kanazawa Energy is a Gold sustaining member of the museum, at 300,000 yen a year per unit on the published scale. The company was founded on 13 May 2021 (as Kanazawa Gas Denki, renamed on 30 November 2021), so any listing of it falls within the last five years (company site).

Kanazawa Energy supplies city gas, runs five hydropower plants taken over from the city, and sells electricity; gas and hydropower operations began on 1 April 2022 (company site). The company site names its main shareholders as Hokuriku Electric Power, Toho Gas, the city of Kanazawa, Hokkoku Bank, Hokkoku Shimbun, Matsumura Bussan and Komatsu Gas, without percentages.

Unverified: ownership split of Hokuriku Electric Power 48%, Toho Gas 43%, the city of Kanazawa 3% and Hokkoku Bank and Hokkoku Shimbun 2% each, from pedia.3rd-in.co.jp, an unofficial encyclopedia site; the company site gives no percentages.

Iwatani Central Hokuriku is a Standard member, listed in the single Standard list. It is an LP gas retailer in Ishikawa, Toyama and Fukui prefectures (Be Connect Hokuriku company directory; enepi.jp, citing the 2022 LP Gas Yearbook); its own site showed a maintenance notice when opened.

press.overall: Very little criticism. The one critical piece found dates from the museum's opening year and concerns the building and the museum's idea of itself.

items.title: Kieran Long, "21st Century Museum" (issue 020, February 2005; web page dated 23 March 2007)
points: "The biggest criticism" is that SANAA's Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa "ask us to believe in the building's architectural conceits" instead of making visitors feel their effects; with its monochrome colour scheme and long corridors it is "more like being in a highly-appointed hospital".

"Liberalism of this kind includes people but does not empower them"; Long calls the museum's description of itself, which appeals to an undefined and vague common consciousness, "in the final reckoning banal".
Long doubts a collection shaped by consensus will be "of enduring quality" and calls the museum "more like a curiosity shop". The same piece calls the architecture "quietly radical".

details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum is mainly the city of Kanazawa, which is not a red flag by itself. The weak point is a gas utility, Kanazawa Energy, among its top-tier sustaining members, with an ownership split that comes from a non-official source; the amount it paid is not published. Worth watching: the museum's planned 2027 closure and whether it publishes accounts and a funder list with dates.

name: Gotoh Museum
funding: The museum's site says it is a public interest incorporated foundation and does not state funders (museum website). A 2026 guide says it houses the private collection of Keita Gotoh, chairman of the Tokyu Group (Conde House Japan, 4 September 2026).
watch: A foundation museum opened in 1960 for the collection of Tokyu Group chairman Keita Gotoh, holding part of the 12th-century Genji Monogatari Emaki, shown for about a week each Golden Week.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts.

overview: The Gotoh Museum is at 3-9-25 Kaminoge, Setagaya-ku, Tokyo, and is a public interest incorporated foundation (museum website).
It opened in 1960 for the private collection of Keita Gotoh, chairman of the Tokyu Group (Conde House Japan, 4 September 2026).

What is there: the Genji Monogatari Emaki and the Murasaki Shikibu Diary Emaki, paintings, calligraphy, tea utensils, ceramics and archaeological items; the Genji fragments are described as the oldest surviving illustrated handscroll of the Tale of Genji and are shown for about a week in Golden Week, the diary fragments each autumn (museum website; Conde House Japan, 4 September 2026).
Archive: the collection includes the Tokyu Kokusyo Bunko (Daito Kyu Kinen Bunko); the page does not describe it further (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Gotoh Museum: private: a foundation holding a Tokyu chairman's collection; the pages read name no funders
funding: The museum is a public interest incorporated foundation (museum website).
No reporting found of grants, sponsors or accounts in the pages read.
details.bottom_line: A Tokyu founder's collection run by a foundation; the pages read give no amounts. Check the foundation's public disclosures.

name: New National Theatre Tokyo (NNTT)
funding: The page read names Special Corporate Sponsors for 2026/2027, including Onward, Toyota, TBS and Nippon Life, and a Patronage and Support section; it does not give amounts or the public subsidy.
watch: Japan's national theatre for opera, ballet and dance, and drama, run by the New National Theatre Foundation (president Zeniya Masami); it opened in autumn 1997.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Publishes annual reports for 2017 to 2024 for download (theatre website).

overview: Japan's national theatre for the contemporary performing arts, in Tokyo (theatre website).
Opened autumn 1997; operated by the New National Theatre Foundation (theatre website).

What is there: opera with the NNT Chorus and Opera Studio, ballet and dance with the National Ballet of Japan and the NNT Ballet School, and the NNT Drama Studio; more than 750 productions since opening, about 300 performances a season running October to July (theatre website).
Archive: an Information Centre is listed among the facilities; annual reports for 2017 to 2024 are downloadable (theatre website).
details.funding_verdict: New National Theatre Tokyo: public foundation with corporate sponsors, amounts not seen
funding: Special Corporate Sponsors 2026/2027 include Onward, Toyota, TBS and Nippon Life (theatre website).
The page read did not give the government subsidy, ticket income or sponsor amounts.
details.bottom_line: Sponsors are named but no figures were read. The annual reports on the theatre's site are the place to find the subsidy and sponsor income.

name: Okayama Art Summit
funding: Okayama City, Okayama Prefecture and the Ishikawa Foundation lead the executive committee. Stripe International and Chugoku Bank are corporate partners. Foundation president Yasuharu Ishikawa directs the Summit.
watch: Citizens petitioned the city council and prefecture in 2021 and 2022 over harassment allegations against Ishikawa. Both were rejected; he directs the 2025 edition.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: The 2025 summit site names its executive committee, sponsors and supporting agencies by name.
affiliations_note: The Okayama Art Summit is run by an executive committee with the Okayama Culture Zone Liaison Council, the Consortium of Universities in Okayama and Okayama University as affiliated bodies. Listed in the Biennial Foundation directory.

overview: Contemporary art festival in Okayama City, created to revive the old castle town area around Okayama Castle and Korakuen Garden. The first edition ran from 9 October to 27 November 2016 on the theme "Development", with Liam Gillick as artistic director (festival website).
Organised by the Okayama Art Summit Executive Committee, chaired by Okayama's mayor Masao Omori (festival website).

Rirkrit Tiravanija was artistic director of the 2022 edition (30 September to 27 November 2022). Philippe Parreno, appointed on 24 October 2023, directed the 2025 edition, The Parks of Aomame, from 26 September to 24 November 2025 with thirty individuals and groups from twelve countries and regions (e-flux).
Admission was free in 2025. The festival site announces the next edition for 2028 (news item of 30 March 2026).
Yasuharu Ishikawa, president of the Ishikawa Foundation, is executive producer of the 2025 edition and Taro Nasu of the gallery TARO NASU is executive director (festival website).
details.funding_verdict: Okayama Art Summit: public and corporate: Okayama City and Prefecture, the Ishikawa Foundation, and named sponsors
funding: The executive committee consists mainly of Okayama City, Okayama Prefecture and the Ishikawa Foundation (Tokyo Art Beat, Natsuko Fukushima, 19 October 2022).

The 2025 about page lists Merco Group as co-organizer; Special Sponsors Ishikawa Holdings, Sanyo Shimbun, Chugin Financial Group and JR West Group; and Sponsors Okayama Toyota Group, Sapix, Tomiya Corporation, Nakashima Holdings, JT, Ryobi Group, RSK, OHK, TSC, ProdCo, Okayama University of Science and Maruzen-Yushodo. Granting Agencies are the Social Creation Arts Fund and Institut Français.

red_flags.heading: Tobacco
points: The 2025 edition's about page lists "JT" among the Sponsors, the tier below Special Sponsors. The page gives the name only as "JT"; the logo links to jti.co.jp, which Wikipedia gives as the website of Japan Tobacco, a tobacco company.

red_flags.heading: Citizen petitions over executive producer Yasuharu Ishikawa
points: Petitioners: the Okayama Citizens' Association for Okayama Art Summit, formed in August 2021. It asked that Ishikawa be replaced as general producer by an expert with ties to Okayama and that the festival concept be reviewed (Tokyo Art Beat, 24 November 2021 and 19 October 2022).

Background: multiple harassment accusations against Ishikawa, then head of the fashion company Stripe International, were reported for August 2015 to May 2018. He received a "stern warning" in December 2018 with no disciplinary action, did not admit harassment and resigned as company president in March 2020 (Tokyo Art Beat, 19 October 2022).

Dates: petition to Okayama City Council on 19 November 2021, withdrawn 24 November; to the Prefectural Assembly on 22 February 2022 and the City Council on 25 February. The City Council's Citizens and Industry Committee rejected it on 9 March 2022 and the Prefectural Assembly's Environment, Culture, Health and Welfare Committee on 15 March (Tokyo Art Beat, 24 November 2021, updated 18 August 2022).

On 8 July 2022 the group submitted a request with 400 signatures; on 15 July the city replied that it would "do its best to find an alternative venue" and did not address the harassment allegations (Tokyo Art Beat, 19 October 2022).

On 27 September 2022 the executive committee said an extraordinary investigation committee at Stripe did not find harassment by Ishikawa, that it saw no need to explain to citizens or share information with participating artists, and answered "not applicable" when asked for Tiravanija's view (Tokyo Art Beat, title translated).
The Ishikawa Foundation, of which Ishikawa is president, sits on the executive committee (Tokyo Art Beat, 19 October 2022).

press.overall: Tokyo Art Beat covered the petitions and the committee's answers; one essay criticises the organisers' lack of explanation.

items.title: Natsuko Fukushima, "Controversy Brews Over Rirkrit Tiravanija's 'Okayama Art Summit': Who Does the 'Communication' Exclude?" (19 October 2022)
points: Asks how citizens can be recognised and dialogue begin when the organisers claim no knowledge of the group.

Reports that Tiravanija said at the 29 September 2022 press conference, "I am not aware of a group in Okayama", and that Nasu said, "I personally do not know any details regarding the citizen's group".

items.title: Natsuko Fukushima, "Citizen Petitions and Requests Regarding 'Okayama Art Summit 2022': Questions and Answers with the Executive Committee" (27 September 2022, in Japanese; title translated)
points: Not criticism: records the committee's written answers.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the festival is local public and corporate: Okayama City and Prefecture, the Ishikawa Foundation, and regional sponsors. Documented points are the 2025 Sponsors listing of "JT" and the 2021 and 2022 citizen petitions against executive producer Yasuharu Ishikawa, which committees of the city council and prefectural assembly rejected in March 2022.

name: Pola Museum of Art
funding: Pola Art Foundation, set up in May 1996 with the personal assets of Tsuneji Suzuki of the Pola founding family; a public-interest foundation since July 2010.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The Pola Art Foundation posts business reports for FY2021 to FY2025, balance sheets and net-asset statements; a board list.
finances_note: FY2025 income JPY 4.93B: about 83 percent endowment dividends, 16 percent earned museum revenue, 1 percent other; no grant or donation line (net-assets statement).
affiliations_note: Pola Museum of Art is run by the Pola Art Foundation, established in 1996, and was built from the collection of Pola head Tsuneshi Suzuki.

overview: Art museum at 1285 Sengokuhara, Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture, in Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park (e-flux directory; English Wikipedia).
Opened in September 2002, run by the Pola Art Foundation (Japanese Wikipedia). The foundation was established in 1996 (Mecenat Association).
Built to show about 9,500 works collected over decades by Tsuneji Suzuki, second head of the Pola founding family. The collection now numbers about 10,000 (Japanese Wikipedia).
Designed by Nikken Sekkei and built by Takenaka Corporation (Japanese Wikipedia). Most of the building sits underground. Only the glass atrium shows above the forest floor (Alan Gleason, Artscape).

Collection: French Impressionist and École de Paris painting, Western and Japanese-style paintings, prints, East Asian ceramics, glass and cosmetic tools (English Wikipedia; e-flux directory). A 670-metre nature trail was added in 2013 (English Wikipedia).
Visiting: the museum's own notice gives hours of 9:00 to 17:00 with last admission at 16:30.
details.funding_verdict: Pola Museum of Art: foundation-run: the Pola Art Foundation, with a collection gathered by Tsuneji Suzuki of the Pola founding family
funding: The Pola Art Foundation operates the museum and also runs overseas internships for young artists, research programmes for curators and international exchange (Mecenat Association).

Japanese Wikipedia says the museum opened in September 2002 to display the collection of Tsuneji Suzuki, second head of the Pola founding family; English Wikipedia says the works were acquired by the former head of the Pola cosmetics group.
details.bottom_line: The museum is operated by the Pola Art Foundation, established in 1996 (Mecenat Association), and displays the collection of Tsuneji Suzuki, second head of the Pola founding family (Japanese Wikipedia). The foundation also runs internships for young artists, programmes for curators and international exchange.

name: Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum
funding: The page read says the museum was founded through a donation from the businessman Sato Keitaro, known as the coal god; it did not state the current operator or funding.
watch: Opened in 1926 as Japan's first public art museum, with a founding gift from Sato Keitaro (museum website).
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The page read showed no published accounts.

overview: A public art museum in Ueno Park, Tokyo (museum website).
Opened in 1926 as Japan's first public art museum; founded through a donation from Sato Keitaro, a businessman from northern Kyushu known as the coal god (museum website).
What is there: the page read did not describe the collection.
Archive: the page read did not mention an art library or archive.
details.funding_verdict: Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum: founded by a private gift, current funding not stated in the page read
funding: Founding gift from Sato Keitaro, businessman known as the coal god (museum website). No amount or year other than 1926 was given.
The page read did not name the operator or give any grant figures.
details.bottom_line: The founding money was one businessman's gift. Who pays now was not stated on the page read.

name: The Jordan Museum
funding: The pages read did not state who funds it. The National (13 March 2014) said some displays were on loan from the Department of Antiquities and did not name municipal, ministry or donor funding.
watch: Jordan's largest museum, nearly 10,000 square metres, showing the 'Ain Ghazal plaster statues of about 7500 BC and Dead Sea Scrolls material. The pages read did not name its funders.
records_note: No accounts seen in the pages read.

overview: The country's largest museum at nearly 10,000 square metres, in Amman (The National, 13 March 2014).
A soft opening took place in January 2013 with the grand opening pending in March 2014; director Sharifa Nofa Bint Nasser (The National, 13 March 2014).

What is there: exhibits from the Stone Age to modern Jordan, animal bones 1.5 million years old, a double-headed plaster statue of 7500 BC from 'Ain Ghazal, human-shaped clay coffins, a replica Moabite basalt stone, and Dead Sea Scrolls material on loan from the Department of Antiquities (The National, 13 March 2014).
Archive: the pages read did not describe a library or archive. The museum's own site was under redevelopment.
details.funding_verdict: The Jordan Museum: public in the pages read; no amounts found.
funding: Some displays are on loan from the Department of Antiquities (The National, 13 March 2014).
No reporting found, in the pages read, of the builder, donors or operating budget.
details.bottom_line: The pages read give no funding information. The 'Ain Ghazal statues and scroll display are the draws; the Department of Antiquities lends material.
